title: Complainant walks out of inquiry, says it's flawed
article: Julie Berg, the complainant who triggered an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding her brother's death while in police custody, stomped out of the hearing Tuesday, calling the public process "badly flawed."

Accompanied by her lawyer, Cameron Ward, the woman told reporters her action was to protest her "limited standing" status at the hearing, which basically allows her to be an observer rather than a full participant.
"I have very limited standing and this is just the beginning of, I'm afraid to say it, a very flawed process," she said outside court.

"I feel it's absolutely unfair for myself as a complainant. This isn't just for me, it's for the public. That's the whole purpose of a public hearing. For me as a complainant, I have no standing -- I don't see what I will get out of this."
Ward said he and his client will ponder their next move.
"We will meet to consider implications of the \[adjudicator's\] ruling," the lawyer said. "We're not ruling anything out."
Berg said she was incensed over being refused input on a so- called agreed statement of facts that was to be read into the record by commission counsel Dana Urban -- a statement she disagrees with.

The hearing, undertaken by B.C.'s Police Complaint Commissioner, is a quasi-judicial proceeding that will determine whether Vancouver police Const. David Bruce-Thomas abused his authority by using excessive force while arresting Jeffrey Michael Berg in August 2000 on Slocan Street in east Vancouver.
Ward said he was faxed a copy of the eight-page statement -- drawn up by Urban and Bruce-Thomas's lawyer, Bill Smart -- only two hours before the hearing opened at 10 a.m.

"I was not included in the negotiations and discussions that led to that so called agreed statement of facts," Ward said. "When I looked at it, I could see some clear errors, flaws and problems, so I objected to it."
Ward charged that the statement includes evidence no court would allow, inaccurate statements and omissions.
Smart told the hearing Tuesday the process could take days or even weeks longer if the statement wasn't accepted.
In the end, commission adjudicator Brian Weddell, a retired provincial court judge, allowed the statement to be read into the record.
A coroner's jury earlier ruled Jeffrey Berg's death a homicide, a neutral term that does not attach blame but indicates that one person was killed by another.

An autopsy showed Berg, 37, a home-invasion suspect, died as a result of a blow to the neck, which caused an aneurysm and led to a fatal heart attack. He also suffered head injuries and a badly bruised testicle.

Witness Bob Gullachsen, who lived in the neighbourhood where the arrest took place, testified Tuesday that he saw a lone police officer drag a handcuffed man face down on the pavement across the alley behind a townhouse complex.
"The officer had him by the handcuffs, hands bound behind his back, and dragged him across the alley," said Gullachsen, 27, who said he watched the scene from his balcony.
"I was quite shocked and went back inside. I was pretty surprised this was happening right outside my house. I never saw the guy move. He was completely helpless."
